skill.name: uniprot-database
skill.description: Query UniProt through its REST API for protein searches, entry retrieval, FASTA export, field selection, streaming, and cross-database identifier mapping.
skill.summary: Search and retrieve UniProt protein data with REST guidance and a Python client.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: All 129 static alerts are false positives after contextual review. Backtick alerts are Markdown or JavaScript literals; network calls target documented UniProt endpoints, while file writes are explicit download examples. The Python ID-mapping helper has unbounded polling and lacks request timeouts, creating a low-severity availability risk.

remediation.suggestion: Set HTTP timeouts and a maximum polling deadline. Return a clear timeout error when UniProt does not complete a mapping job.

semantic_findings.title: Unbounded ID-mapping polling
semantic_findings.description: The ID-mapping loop has no maximum attempts, and requests omit timeouts. A stalled API can keep an agent process occupied indefinitely.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The loop condition is unconditional and has no deadline or attempt limit. The surrounding requests also omit timeout arguments.

content.value_statement: Protein searches and identifier mapping often require careful UniProt REST syntax. This skill provides focused guidance and a Python client for reliable retrieval.
actual_capabilities: Search UniProt by protein name, gene, accession, organism, taxonomy, annotation, or sequence properties.
Retrieve individual protein entries in JSON, TSV, XML, FASTA, RDF, Excel, or text formats.
Map identifiers between UniProt and supported resources such as Ensembl, RefSeq, PDB, and Gene Ontology.
Select specific annotation fields to reduce response size and simplify downstream analysis.
Stream large query results and batch multiple accession searches through the provided Python client.
limitations: Internet access to public UniProt endpoints is required.
API availability, schemas, limits, and supported mapping databases can change outside this skill.
ID-mapping jobs accept at most 100,000 identifiers and remain available for seven days.
The client does not interpret biological evidence or replace expert review of protein annotations.

use_cases.title: Retrieve proteins for experiments
use_cases.description: Find reviewed entries and FASTA sequences for genes or proteins selected during experimental planning.

use_cases.title: Normalize identifiers for analysis
use_cases.description: Convert mixed protein identifiers into UniProt accessions before merging datasets or running pipelines.

use_cases.title: Teach reproducible database queries
use_cases.description: Demonstrate field selection, review-status filters, pagination, and output formats with clear UniProt examples.

prompt_templates.title: Find a protein entry
prompt_templates.prompt: Find UniProt entry {accession}. Return its reviewed status, protein name, organism, gene names, sequence length, and available functional summary.

prompt_templates.title: Search reviewed proteins
prompt_templates.prompt: Search UniProt for reviewed {protein_family} proteins in {organism}. Return up to {limit} accessions with gene names, lengths, and functions.

prompt_templates.title: Map database identifiers
prompt_templates.prompt: Map these {source_database} identifiers to {target_database}: {identifiers}. Report successful mappings, failed identifiers, duplicate mappings, and relevant UniProt accessions.

prompt_templates.title: Design a reproducible dataset
prompt_templates.scenario: Plan an advanced, bounded retrieval workflow.
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a UniProt query for {research_question}. Apply {filters}, select only {fields}, explain review status, paginate safely, and summarize data-quality caveats.

output_examples.input: Find the reviewed human insulin precursor entry.
output_examples.output: P01308, INS_HUMAN. Reviewed Swiss-Prot entry for insulin in Homo sapiens; gene INS; sequence length 110 amino acids.

output_examples.input: Map a supplied list of UniProt accessions to PDB.
output_examples.output: A mapping summary lists each accession, matching PDB identifiers, unmapped inputs, and cases where one protein maps to multiple structures.

output_examples.input: Find five reviewed human kinases with known structures.
output_examples.output: A compact table lists five accessions with gene names, protein names, sequence lengths, and PDB cross-references.

best_practices: Prefer reviewed Swiss-Prot entries when curated evidence is required.
Request only needed fields and use bounded result sizes before streaming complete datasets.
Record the query, selected fields, output format, and retrieval date for reproducibility.
anti_patterns: Do not request every annotation field when only sequences or identifiers are needed.
Do not treat unreviewed TrEMBL predictions as manually curated evidence.
Do not submit confidential sequences or identifiers to public UniProt endpoints.

faq.question: Does this skill require a UniProt API key?
faq.answer: No. The documented public UniProt REST endpoints do not require an API key for these operations.

faq.question: Which output formats are supported?
faq.answer: The references cover JSON, TSV, Excel, XML, FASTA, RDF, and text, with operation-specific availability.

faq.question: Can it map identifiers from other databases?
faq.answer: Yes. It supports UniProt ID mapping for resources including Ensembl, RefSeq, PDB, EMBL, and Gene Ontology.

faq.question: Can it retrieve large protein datasets?
faq.answer: Yes. The stream endpoint returns complete result sets, while search requests support smaller paginated responses.

faq.question: Does it verify biological conclusions?
faq.answer: No. It retrieves annotations and sequences but does not validate experimental evidence or clinical significance.

faq.question: Can the examples write files?
faq.answer: Yes. Download examples write requested UniProt responses to explicit local paths selected by the user.
